A. Three satellites (max. 10 points)

During one night an observer on the Earth (of radius $R = 6378$ km), standing at geographic latitude $\varphi$, noticed an unprecedented phenomenon. He observed, continuously one after another, three satellites orbiting in the plane of the equator, which moved across the sky along the same trajectory, while at every moment he saw exactly one of them (i.e. during the setting of one satellite the next one was rising, and so on three times until the cycle repeated).

a) Determine at what height $h$ above the Earth's surface such satellites move.

b) Calculate the altitude $\alpha$ of a satellite above the horizon at the time of its culmination.

c) Determine the period $\tau$ with which the whole cycle will repeat.

Compute numerically for an observer in Prague ($\varphi = 50^\circ\,05'$) and in Bogotá ($\varphi = 4^\circ\,36'$).

B. Amateur (max. 10 points)

An amateur astronomer from Opava heard about the discovery of a new triple-star system. So he took his Cassegrain telescope (with a primary mirror of diameter $D_1 = 203$ mm and a secondary mirror of diameter $D_2 = 64$ mm) and went to observe in the Beskydy dark-sky area. We know about the triple star that its components have magnitudes $14^\mathrm{m}$, $14.5^\mathrm{m}$ and $16^\mathrm{m}$, and that they are so close together that the telescope cannot resolve them. Calculate the limiting magnitude $m_\mathrm{D}$ for the astronomer's telescope, then the magnitude $m_*$ of the triple-star system, and on the basis of your results decide whether the astronomer can observe the triple star with his telescope.

C. Meson decay (max. 10 points)

A meson $\pi^0$ with rest mass $m_0$ decays into two photons, $\pi^0 \to \gamma\gamma$. If we denote by $E$ the total energy of the meson with respect to the laboratory frame (LAB), determine:

1. the energies of both photons $E_1$, $E_2$ as functions of $E$, $m_0$ and the decay angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$, which express the deviation of the direction of flight of both photons from the original trajectory of the meson,

2. the magnitude of the velocity $v$ of the meson with respect to LAB, if $E_1 = E_\mathrm{max}$ and $E_2 = E_\mathrm{min}$, i.e. one photon had the smallest possible energy it could have and the other photon, on the contrary, had the largest possible energy. Express the result in terms of the quantities $E_\mathrm{max}$, $E_\mathrm{min}$ and the speed of light $c$.

D. Global storm (max. 10 points)

A dust storm broke out on Mars which uniformly covered the whole surface of the planet so that it dimmed the magnitude of the Sun at the zenith by $\Delta m = 0.5$ mag. Assuming that the dust grains have a radius $r = 0.5$ mm and a density $\rho = 1.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, determine (an order of magnitude is enough) the total mass $M$ of the dust particles in the Martian atmosphere (in kg).

E. Spy satellite (max. 20 points)

Consider an artificial satellite orbiting the Earth on a circular orbit in the plane of the equator in the direction of the Earth's rotation. The satellite orbits at a height $H = 500$ km above the Earth's surface. For the purpose of this problem assume that the Earth has the shape of an ideal sphere of radius $R_\mathrm{Z} = 6371$ km and mass $M_\mathrm{Z} = 5.972\cdot10^{24}$ kg. Further denote by $T_0 = 23^\mathrm{h}\,56^\mathrm{m}\,4^\mathrm{s}$ the sidereal rotation period of the Earth.

a) Calculate the geocentric speed $u$ of the motion of an observer on the equator on the Earth's surface. Assume that the observer does not move with respect to the Earth's surface. Express the result both in general in terms of $R_\mathrm{Z}$ and $T_0$ and numerically in $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

b) Calculate the orbital speed $v$ and the orbital period $T$ of the satellite. Express the results in general in terms of $G$, $M_\mathrm{Z}$, $R_\mathrm{Z}$, $H$ (where $G$ is Newton's gravitational constant) and numerically (in $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and in hours respectively).

Now consider that the task of the satellite is spying on various targets on the Earth's surface.

c) Determine the maximum and minimum geographic latitude $\pm|\varphi_\mathrm{max}|$ of the places that the satellite can watch. Give the numerical value in degrees. Will refraction theoretically enlarge or reduce this region?

In the rest of the problem neglect atmospheric refraction.

d) What fraction $p$ of the Earth's surface can the satellite watch at one moment? What fraction $p'$ of the Earth's surface can the satellite watch in the long term? Express the results in general in terms of $R_\mathrm{Z}$ and $H$ and numerically in percent.

Let us now assume that the target being watched is located on the equator.

e) Determine the period $T_s$ with which the satellite finds itself directly above the target. Express the result in hours.

f) Calculate for how long a time $\Delta T$ within each period $T_s$ the satellite can watch the target. Express the result numerically in minutes. What fraction $\tau$ of the total time is the time during which the satellite can watch the target? Assume ideal weather over the watched target.

g) Express the angle $\alpha(t)$ between the radius vector of the satellite and the line joining the centre of the Earth with the watched target in terms of $t$, $T_s$, $t_i$ and $\Delta T$.

h) Express the angular velocity $\Omega$ with which the camera on board the satellite turns after the target (with respect to the body of the satellite) as a function of time $t \in \langle t_i, t_f\rangle$, where $t_i$ and $t_f$ are the times of the beginning and the end of the visibility of the satellite within each observing window. First carry out the calculation assuming a zero sidereal rotation period of the satellite: show that then one can write
$$\Omega(t) = \frac{2\pi}{T_s}\,\frac{1-\cos|\varphi_\mathrm{max}|\cos\alpha(t)}{1+\cos^2|\varphi_\mathrm{max}| - 2\cos|\varphi_\mathrm{max}|\cos\alpha(t)}. \qquad (1)$$

i) Express the angular velocities of the camera $\Omega_i$, $\Omega_f$ and $\Omega_c$ at the times $t = t_i$, $t = t_f$ and $t = t_c \equiv t_i + \Delta T/2$ in terms of $T_s$ and $\cos|\varphi_\mathrm{max}|$. Calculate their numerical values in degrees per second.

j) How would the results for $\Omega(t)$, $\Omega_i$, $\Omega_f$ and $\Omega_c$ change assuming synchronous rotation of the satellite (sidereal rotation period of the satellite equal to $T_0$ in the direction of the satellite's orbital motion)?

Note: parts i) and j) may be solved using relation (1) for $\Omega(t)$ without a point penalty, even if you did not manage to derive it in part h).

F. Greenhouse effect (max. 20 points)

Consider an exoplanet of radius $R_e$ orbiting its central star on a circular orbit at a distance $d$. Denote the luminosity of the central star by $L_*$. Assume that the exoplanet is a perfect sphere with surface albedo $A$ and has no internal source of heat.

a) Calculate the surface temperature $T_{e1}$ of the exoplanet if we assume that the rotation period of the exoplanet about its axis is so short that we can consider the same temperature over the whole surface. Express the result in terms of the given quantities and the Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma$.

So far we have assumed that the exoplanet has no atmosphere. But how would the result change if we took an atmosphere into account? Let us model the atmosphere as a thin spherical layer above the surface of the planet which has different transmission coefficients¹ for radiation coming from the star (whether falling directly on the atmosphere or reflected from the surface of the exoplanet) and for radiation emitted by the exoplanet as a consequence of maintaining thermal equilibrium. Denote these transmission coefficients $t_*$ and $t_e$ respectively, $t_* \neq t_e$, and assume that their value is independent of the angle of incidence of the incoming radiation and that both are in general non-zero.

b) Show that the equation of thermal equilibrium in the case of our simple model of the atmosphere is modified into the following form
$$\frac{t_*(1-A)}{1-A(1-t_*)}\,\frac{L_*}{4\pi d^2}\,\pi R_e^2 = \frac{t_e}{1-A(1-t_e)}\,4\pi R_e^2 T_{e2}^4\,\sigma, \qquad (3)$$
where on the left-hand side of the equation we have the radiant power received by the surface of the exoplanet and on the right-hand side the radiant power emitted by the surface of the exoplanet. Compared with the usual form of this equation, terms appear here that modify the amount of received and emitted power because of the presence of the atmosphere. When calculating the multiple reflection of radiation from the atmosphere and the surface of the planet it might be useful to know that for $0 < |q| < 1$
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a q^n = \frac{a}{1-q}.$$

c) What is the equilibrium thermodynamic temperature $T_{e2}$ of the exoplanet in the case of the presence of an atmosphere described by the simple model given above in the statement?

d) What must be the relation between the transmission coefficients $t_*$ and $t_e$ for us to be able to observe the greenhouse effect, i.e. an increase of temperature compared with the situation without an atmosphere?

e) If $t_* = t_e$ were to occur, how would this affect the surface temperature of the exoplanet? Compare with the results of the previous parts.

¹ The transmission coefficient $t$ of a thin layer is a real number taking values in the interval $[0, 1]$ and expresses what part of the radiation passes through this layer. The radiation that does not pass through is reflected back. The part of the radiation reflected back is usually denoted $r$, and $t + r = 1$, which means that the layer itself does not heat up.

G. V838 Monocerotis (max. 40 points)

At the beginning of 2002 the star V838 Mon exploded, and it immediately became an object of interest for astronomers. The outburst reached its maximum on 6 February 2002. In the following months the Hubble Space Telescope took several photographs of the light echo around the star. This very rare phenomenon can be used to estimate the distance to the object, which we shall also try to do in this problem.

A light echo arises when a strong flash from a source is reflected by interstellar dust. If we assume that each photon is reflected exactly once, we conclude that the illuminated dust must satisfy the equality $r + l = d + ct$, where $r$ is the distance of the illuminated dust from the source of radiation, $l$ is the distance of the illuminated dust from the observer, $d$ is the distance between the source and the observer and $t$ is the time that has elapsed since the observed flash. From this equality one can easily see that the illuminated dust lies on an ellipsoid with foci at the source and at the observer.

In our case we shall assume that the star was surrounded by several spherical dust shells, on which the light echo forms bright rings. For the radius $r_e$ of such a ring, belonging to a shell of radius $r_0$, at time $t$ after the observed outburst we obtain the relation $r_e = \sqrt{2r_0ct - c^2t^2}$, from which the growth rate of the radius $r_e$ can be derived as
$$v = \frac{r_0c - c^2t}{\sqrt{2r_0ct - c^2t^2}}.$$

Figure 1 shows two photographs of the light echo taken by the Hubble Space Telescope; the upper one is in the B filter from 30. 4. 2002 and the lower one is from 20. 5. 2002 and was made by combining photographs in the B, V and I filters. Your task will be to identify on both photographs the rings that correspond to the same dust shell, to measure the angular rate of expansion of the ring and to estimate the distance of the star from a suitable dependence of the angular expansion rate on the angular radius.

a) Express the angular rate of expansion of one ring in terms of its angular radius $\theta$, the time since the observed outburst $t$, the distance of the star from the observer $d$ and the speed of light $c$.

b) Identify on both images at least five pairs of rings that belong to the same shell. On both images measure the radius of these rings at at least five points. From these measurements determine the mean radius of each ring and calculate the angular rate of expansion.

c) Draw a graph of the dependence of $\omega\theta$ on $\theta^2$ for the time $t = 93$ days. For the angular size take the mean value.

d) Using the method of least squares, fit the points in the graph with a suitable straight line.

Method of least squares: if we fit data $(x_i, y_i)$ for $i = 1, \dots, N$ with a straight line $y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i$ (where the values $x_i$ are plotted on the $x$ axis and the values $y_i$ on the $y$ axis), then the mean values $\overline{\beta}$, $\overline{\alpha}$ of the parameters $\beta$, $\alpha$ of this line are found from the relations
$$\overline{\beta} = \frac{N\sigma_{xy} - \sigma_x\sigma_y}{N\sigma_{xx} - \sigma_x^2} \quad\text{and}\quad \overline{\alpha} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\sigma_y - \overline{\beta}\sigma_x\right),$$
where $\sigma_x = \sum_i x_i$, $\sigma_y = \sum_i y_i$, $\sigma_{xy} = \sum_i x_iy_i$, $\sigma_{xx} = \sum_i x_i^2$ and $\sigma_{yy} = \sum_i y_i^2$.

e) Using a suitable reading from the graph, determine the distance of the star V838 Mon.

A. The Earth from afar (max. 10 points)

At what largest angular distance $\alpha$ from a star of apparent magnitude $m = 4.0$ mag could we observe a planet that receives the same amount of radiation as the Earth?

B. Black radiation (max. 10 points)

Determine the wavelength $\lambda_{\max}$ of the maximum of Hawking radiation in multiples of the Schwarzschild radius $R_S$. The temperature of Hawking radiation is calculated as $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$, where $M$ is the mass of the black hole.

C. Volcanic explosion (max. 10 points)

On 15 January 2022 the submarine volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai in the southern Pacific exploded. The consequences of this eruption also appeared in the measurements of atmospheric pressure at the ČHMÚ station in Prague-Libuš, where the first pressure wave was registered on the same day at 19:29. The second pressure wave came from the opposite direction exactly 6 hours later, i.e. the following day at 01:29 in the morning. Assume that the wave propagates at the speed of sound $c_s = 343\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

a) Calculate the distance $d$ of the volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai from Prague.

Further, suppose that the azimuth $A = 33.8^\circ$ of the direction from which the first shock wave came was determined (measured from the north). The geographic coordinates of the Prague-Libuš station are $\varphi_P = 50.0077^\circ$ N and $\lambda_P = 14.4467^\circ$ E.

b) Determine the geographic coordinates $(\varphi_s, \lambda_s)$ of the volcano.

D. Eternal sunset (max. 10 points)

Calculate how the eccentricity of the Earth's orbit would have to change (keeping the value of the semi-major axis and the rotation period) so that at some moment the Sun would start to move across the sky from west to east. Consider the present orbit of the Earth to be exactly circular. Also determine the length $r_p$ of the radius vector at perihelion of the new orbit in multiples of the solar radius.

Hint: write the resulting eccentricity $e$ in the form $e = 1 - \eta$, where you can expect $\eta \ll 1$.

E. The Lagrange point L2 (max. 20 points)

In this problem we will study the motion of a satellite of mass $\mu$ in the vicinity of the Lagrange point L2 of a system of two bodies of masses $M$ and $m$. For simplicity we will consider the mass hierarchy $M \gg m \gg \mu$. Introducing the parameter $\lambda = m/M$, we can therefore assume $\lambda \ll 1$.

a) Write the angular frequency $\omega$ of the orbital motion of the bodies $M$ and $m$ about the centre of mass of the system if they are separated by a constant distance $a$. Express the result in terms of $G$, $M$, $a$ and the parameter $\lambda$.

b) Determine the distances $R$ and $r$ of the body $M$ and of the body $m$, respectively, from the centre of mass. Express the results in terms of $a$ and $\lambda$.

Lagrange points are defined as the places where, in the non-inertial reference frame co-rotating with the system of bodies $m$ and $M$, the total gravitational force acting on a test particle $\mu$ is balanced by the centrifugal force. The Lagrange point L2 lies on the line joining the bodies $M$ and $m$, beyond the less massive body $m$. Let us denote the distance of the point L2 from the body $m$ by $d$ and introduce the parameter $\delta = d/a$. For $M \gg m$ we can assume $d \ll a$.

c) Express the centrifugal acceleration $a_{o,L2}$ acting on a test particle placed at L2 in terms of $G$, $M$, $a$, $\lambda$ and $\delta$. Neglect terms in which small quantities are multiplied together.

d) Express the total gravitational acceleration $a_{g,L2}$ acting on a test particle $\mu$ placed at L2 in terms of $G$, $M$, $a$, $\lambda$ and $\delta$. To simplify the contributions of the heavier of the bodies, use the binomial approximation $(1+x)^p \approx 1 + px$, valid for $x \ll 1$.

e) Use the balance of the total gravitational and centrifugal forces acting on a static test particle $\mu$ placed at L2 to express the parameter $\delta$ as a function of $\lambda$: show that $\delta = (\lambda/3)^{1/3}$.

f) Calculate the value of the parameter $\delta$ for the binary systems Sun–Earth and Earth–Moon.

g) For both of these binary systems also determine the value of the distance $d$ of the point L2 from the less massive body.

h) Compare the angular sizes $\alpha_Z$ and $\alpha_M$ of the Earth and the Moon as they would be seen by an observer at the point L2 of the Earth–Moon system.

If we slightly displaced the test particle from the point L2, we would find that along the line joining $M$ and $m$ it would tend to move away from L2, whereas in both perpendicular directions it would tend to return to L2. The analysis of trajectories around the point L2 is further complicated by the fact that a body moving in a non-inertial reference frame is acted on by the Coriolis force. With a suitable choice of initial conditions one can obtain orbits that stay in the vicinity of L2: for small displacements these trajectories have the shape of three-dimensional Lissajous figures; for larger displacements we would obtain, for example, the so-called halo orbit, along which the recently launched JWST telescope also moves.

In the rest of the problem we will deal with a simplified situation in which the test particle is displaced from the point L2 perpendicular to the orbital plane of the bodies $M$ and $m$ by a small distance $h \ll d \ll a$: in this case the Coriolis force is always zero. Introducing the parameter $\chi = h/d$, we can therefore assume $\chi \ll 1$.

i) Determine the total acceleration $a_h$ acting on the test particle displaced in this way, in the direction perpendicular to the orbital plane of the bodies $M$ and $m$. Using the condition $\chi \ll 1$, write the result in the approximate form $-\Omega^2 h$, where the constant $\Omega$ is to be expressed as a multiple of $\omega$.

Let us now consider a satellite at rest at the point L2 of the Earth–Moon system.

j) Calculate the minimum value $V$ of the velocity that must be given to the satellite in the direction perpendicular to the plane of the Moon's orbit around the Earth so that it could at least at some time communicate with any place on the Earth's surface.

F. Breakthrough Starshot (max. 20 points)

In this problem we will explore the possibilities of interstellar travel using laser propulsion. Specifically, we will consider a very powerful monochromatic laser with total power $P = 100$ GW and wavelength $\lambda_0 = 650$ nm placed in orbit around the Earth. We then direct the entire power of this laser onto a very light (rest mass $m = 10$ g) perfectly reflecting sail, which we thereby try to accelerate to a non-negligible fraction of the speed of light.

a) Determine the total number of photons $\nu_0$ that fall on the sail per unit time if the sail is at rest with respect to the source of the laser radiation.

b) How does this result change if the sail moves with speed $v$ away from the source? Denote the corresponding number of photons per unit time by $\nu$.

c) For $v \ll c$ calculate the change of momentum of the sail per unit time (i.e. the force $F$ acting on it) in terms of $P$, $c$ and $v$.

d) Using your non-relativistic result for the force, determine the time $t(V)$ it would take to accelerate the sail to the final speed $V = 0.1c$. Express the result in seconds.

In the rest of the problem we will calculate relativistically. We will also distinguish between the time measured in the frame attached to the source of the laser radiation and the time that would be measured by an observer attached to the sail (proper time). It will be convenient to introduce the kinematic parameters of the sail
$$\alpha = \frac{p}{mc}, \qquad \beta = \frac{v}{c}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}},$$
where $p$ denotes the (relativistic) momentum of the sail. Since $p = mv\gamma$, we obtain the relation $\alpha = \beta\gamma$. For the relativistic energy of the sail we then have
$$E = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4} = mc^2\sqrt{1+\alpha^2} = mc^2\gamma.$$
We also introduce the kinematic parameter of the photons $\delta = h/(mc\lambda_0)$.

Consider the collision of a single photon of wavelength $\lambda_0$ with the sail of speed $v$ and rest mass $m$ in the reference frame of the source. The sail moves away from the source of the photons. After the collision the photon will move back towards the source and will have wavelength $\lambda_0'$, while the sail will move with a new speed $v'$.

e) Write the laws of conservation of relativistic momentum and energy of the system before and after the collision in the reference frame of the photon source. Express the momenta and energies of the sail and of the photons before and after the collision in terms of the corresponding parameters $\alpha$, $\delta$ and $\alpha'$, $\delta'$.

f) Express $\alpha' - \alpha$ as a function of $\alpha$ and $\delta$. Simplify the final result assuming that the momenta of individual photons are always very small compared with the momentum of the sail (i.e. $\delta \ll \alpha$). Show that
$$\alpha' - \alpha = 2\delta\,\frac{\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}+\alpha}.$$

g) Express the change of the parameter $\alpha$ of the sail per unit time measured in the laser frame (i.e. the force $f$ in the reference frame of the source, normalised by the factor $mc$). Also give the approximate dependence $f(\alpha)$ for $\alpha \gg 1$ (ultra-relativistic regime).

h) Repeat the calculation of the previous part for the case where time is measured in the frame attached to the sail. Denote the resulting force by $\varphi(\alpha)$.

Suppose that we want to accelerate the sail to the ultra-relativistic final speed $V = 0.999c$.

i) Calculate the corresponding value of the parameter $\alpha(V)$.

j) Determine the times $t$ and $\tau$ needed to accelerate the sail to this speed from the point of view of the rest frame of the photon source and of the rest frame of the sail, respectively. Express the results in days.

Hint: the area under the graph of the parabola $y = x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = a$ is $(1/3)a^3$.

G. Star formation (max. 20 points)

The star formation rate $\dot{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ (where the abbreviation SFR comes from the English Star Formation Rate) describes the time course of star formation in galaxies. It is the total mass of newly formed stars, usually expressed in solar masses per unit area of the galactic disc during one million years (unit $M_\odot\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}\,Myr^{-1}}$). To determine the SFR we usually measure the radiation of stars of spectral classes O and B, because these stars have a relatively short lifetime. Since stars form from gas clouds, the evolution of galaxies is determined by the surface density of gas $\Sigma_{\mathrm{Gas}}$ (unit $M_\odot\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$). A. OPAVA-1 (max. 10 points)

Because of bad weather, the participants of the regional round of the Astronomical Olympiad decided to launch a space telescope into orbit around the Earth. The OPAVA-1 mission boasts a primary mirror of diameter $D = 20$ cm and a sensitive CCD camera that needs only $N = 100$ photons to register a signal. $$M_V = a\left(\log\frac{P}{\mathrm{d}} - 1\right) + b, \qquad (\heartsuit)$$
where $P$ denotes the pulsation period and $M_V$ the mean absolute magnitude in the V filter. Using data of Cepheids with known distances (measured by independent methods), we can find the numerical values of the coefficients $a$, $b$ as (footnote 1) $a = (-2.73 \pm 0.07)$ mag and $b = (-3.97 \pm 0.03)$ mag.

The aim of this problem is to illustrate the so-called Baade–Wesselink method (footnote 2) of determining the distances of Cepheids. As we will see in the tasks below, this method uses, on the one hand, spectroscopic measurements of the radial velocities of the photosphere to determine the time dependence of the linear pulsation velocity, and, on the other hand, photometric or interferometric measurements to determine the changes of the angular diameter of the Cepheid's disc. Combining this information gives a way of determining the distances of Cepheids that does not depend on knowledge of the relation $(\heartsuit)$ between period and luminosity. In this problem we will apply the BW method to determine the distance of one particular galactic Cepheid, which will then serve us to validate the relation $(\heartsuit)$.

The variable star $\ell$ Carinae, with mean observed magnitude $V = 3.75$ mag, is the brightest Cepheid in the sky. Moreover, its relatively long pulsation period $P = 35.560$ d means, according to relation $(\heartsuit)$, a relatively high luminosity and hence also a large radius. We can thus say that the angular size of $\ell$ Car in the sky makes this star an ideal candidate for an interferometric measurement of the dependence of the angular diameter of the disc on the phase (footnote 3) of the pulsation period. This measurement was indeed carried out with the VINCI instrument installed at the VLTI interferometer of the European Southern Observatory. $$\Delta I_\nu = \left(\frac{j_\nu}{\kappa_\nu} - I_\nu\right)\varrho\,\kappa_\nu\,\Delta s\,, \qquad (3)$$

F. The Sachs–Wolfe effect

In this problem we shall examine the influence of structures in the Universe on the cosmic microwave background. Specifically, we shall focus on the shift of the wavelengths of CMB photons when passing through the gravitational field of the seeds of large-scale structures in the very early Universe. The consequences of this shift (we speak of the so-called Sachs–Wolfe effect) show up directly as contributions to the anisotropies in the observed CMB temperature – see Figure 4. We shall see that measuring the size of these anisotropies reveals some interesting information about the structure of matter and the laws of physics in the early Universe.

Figure 4: All-sky map of the anisotropies of the temperature of the relic radiation taken by the PLANCK satellite. Red marks regions of higher temperature, blue on the contrary regions of lower temperature. The size of these fluctuations is of the order of $10\ \mu\mathrm{K}$ around the mean value $\bar{T} \approx 2.73$ K.

In general one can say that photons escaping from a gravitational field lose energy – they undergo a gravitational redshift. The wavelength of a photon, during its transfer from a point with gravitational potential $\Phi_0$ to a point with gravitational potential $\Phi$, changes from the value $\lambda_0$ to the value $\lambda$, where the ratio of $\lambda$ and $\lambda_0$ can be obtained from the relation
$$\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0} \approx 1 + \frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{c^2}\,. \qquad (9)$$
We assume $\Phi \ll c^2$. Differences in the value of the gravitational potential also lead to a different perception of time by different observers: if an observer at a place with gravitational potential $\Phi_0$ measures a time interval $\Delta t_0$, then
$$\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta t_0} \approx 1 + \frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{c^2}\,, \qquad (10)$$
where $\Delta t$ is the corresponding time interval measured by an observer at the place with potential $\Phi$.

On large scales the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic with mean density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter (dark and baryonic). On smaller scales we observe inhomogeneities in the distribution of matter. The density $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter can thus in general be written as $\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, where $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ is a deviation that depends on position. To describe the inhomogeneities it is convenient to introduce the dimensionless quantity
$$\delta_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}}{\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}}\,, \qquad (11)$$
which we call the density contrast. In this problem we shall for simplicity model the inhomogeneities as spherical regions of radius $R$ with homogeneous density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}} > \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$, existing within the surrounding homogeneous and isotropic universe of density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$. We shall work exclusively in the so-called linear regime, in which $|\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}| \ll |\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}|$ and hence $\delta_{\mathrm{m}} \ll 1$.

Let us move to a reference frame whose origin is placed at the centre of the spherical region with homogeneous overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$. Denote by $r$ the distance measured from the centre of the region. To find the gravitational potential $\Phi(r)$ caused by the spherical overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ we can use the fact that, for a spherical mass distribution, only the mass located at radii smaller than $r$ contributes to the gravitational force acting on a test body placed at radius $r$. This mass then behaves as if it were compressed into a point mass placed at the origin. Moreover, the potential $\Phi(r)$ and the corresponding gravitational force must be continuous functions for all $r$.

Using this information we could derive that outside the spherical region of overdensity (i.e. for $r > R$) the potential $\Phi(r)$ can be written as
$$\Phi(r) = -\frac{4}{3}\pi G R^2 \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}\delta_{\mathrm{m}}\frac{R}{r}\,, \qquad (r > R) \qquad (12)$$
while inside the region of overdensity (for $r \leqslant R$) we would obtain for the potential
$$\Phi(r) = 2\pi G R^2 \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}\delta_{\mathrm{m}}\left(\frac{r^2}{3R^2} - 1\right). \qquad (r \leqslant R) \qquad (13)$$

a) Write the relation for the depth $\Delta\Phi = \Phi(\infty) - \Phi(0)$ of the potential well generated by a homogeneous spherical overdensity (express it in terms of $G$, $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$, $R$). [1.5 points]

b) Sketch the graph of the potential $\Phi(r)$ as a function of $r$ for all $r > 0$. In your graph mark clearly the edge $r = R$ of the region of overdensity, the value of the potential at this point, and also the minimum of the gravitational potential (the bottom of the well). [3 points]

Let us now focus on the inhomogeneities that existed in the Universe at the epoch of formation of the CMB, i.e. at the moment of decoupling of the relic radiation from matter. In the following tasks you may assume that our Universe is exactly flat, that the present mean temperature of the CMB is $\bar{T}_0 = 2.73$ K, that the cosmological redshift corresponding to the epoch of CMB formation is $z = 1\,090$, that the present value of the Hubble–Lemaître parameter is $H_0 = 67.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, and that the present fraction of the density of matter in the total density in the Universe is $\Omega_{\mathrm{m},0} = 0.315$.

c) Compute the density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter in the Universe (numerically in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$) at the epoch of CMB formation. [2.5 points]

Let us now try to analyse the relation between the density fluctuations $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$ at the epoch of CMB formation and the observed temperature anisotropies of the CMB at various angular scales. The observed spectrum of fluctuations (size of the temperature fluctuation as a function of its angular size) can be seen in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Observed spectrum of CMB anisotropies (data from the PLANCK mission). The quantity plotted on the vertical axis can, in a very simplified way, be understood as the square of the size $\delta T$ of the observed temperature fluctuation. On the horizontal axis (on the upper edge of the graph) the angular size of the fluctuations on the sky is plotted.

First, assuming adiabaticity of the perturbations of the expansion of the Universe, we can regard regions of overdensity as bubbles of space-time in which the evolution of the Universe lags slightly behind its surroundings: as if regions with a small overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ were characterised by an "older" scale factor $a - \delta a$ instead of $a$, where the deviation $0 < \delta a \ll 1$ is chosen such that
$$\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m},0}\,(a - \delta a)^{-3}\,,$$
while $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m},0}\,a^{-3}$. Since the Universe had a higher temperature at smaller scale factors, we thus obtain a positive contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the difference between the temperature of matter in the region of overdensity and the temperature $\bar{T}$ of matter in the surrounding Universe.

d) Show that one can write the approximate relation
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}}{\bar{T}} \approx \frac{1}{3}\,\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$$
between the adiabatic fluctuation $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ of the CMB temperature, the mean temperature $\bar{T}$ of the relic radiation at the epoch of its formation and the density contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$. You may find it useful that $(1+x)^p \approx 1 + px$ for $x \ll 1$. [2 points]

This, however, is not the only effect contributing to the temperature fluctuations of the CMB: the presence of an overdensity also causes a local slowing of the flow of (cosmological) time due to gravitational time dilation according to relation (10) above. This leads to a further lag in the evolution of the region of overdensity compared with its surroundings, and hence to a further positive contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}}$ to the difference between the temperature of the region of overdensity and its surroundings. In the following tasks consider that the expansion of the Universe at the epoch of CMB formation was dominated by matter, so that $a(t) \propto t^{2/3}$.

e) Show that we can write the approximate relation
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}}}{\bar{T}} \approx \frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\,,$$
where $\Delta\Phi$ is the depth of the gravitational potential well caused by the region of overdensity. [2.5 points]

Finally, an outside observer obtains information about the temperature in the region of overdensity through the photons that escape from it. As already described in the introduction to the problem, these photons undergo a gravitational redshift. The outside observer interprets this as a negative contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{red}}$ to the total temperature fluctuation of the region of overdensity compared with its surroundings.

f) Show that approximately
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{red}}}{\bar{T}} \approx -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\,.$$
Write also the relation for the total temperature fluctuation $\delta T = \delta T_{\mathrm{ad}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{dil}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{red}}$ due to the presence of the region of overdensity in terms of $\bar{T}$, $G$, $R$, $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $c$. [3.5 points]

The partial contribution
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}}{\bar{T}} = \frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{red}}}{\bar{T}} \approx -\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}$$
to the temperature fluctuation, which includes all terms explicitly dependent on the radius $R$ of the region of overdensity, is called the ordinary Sachs–Wolfe effect. (In the literature one also meets the so-called integrated Sachs–Wolfe effect, which, however, we shall not deal with in this problem.) From your result in part f) it should be evident that for sufficiently small values of $R$ the resulting temperature fluctuation is dominated by the adiabatic contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$, whereas for large values of $R$ the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect prevails.

g) Determine the critical value $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ of the radius of the region of overdensity at the epoch of CMB formation (numerically in kpc) for which the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the total temperature fluctuation is comparable with the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect. To what angular radius $\alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$ of the fluctuation would this value correspond on today's sky? Discuss how the value $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ relates to the radius $c/H$ of the Hubble sphere at the epoch of recombination. [3 points]

Hint: Converting linear distances to angular ones is very complicated for large redshifts: for $z \gg 1$ one can no longer naively use Hubble's law to compute the distance, and details of the expansion model we consider come into play. You may instead use the well-known fact that the so-called sound horizon at the moment of decoupling of the CMB radiation from matter, which has a linear size of 133 kpc, corresponds on today's sky to an angular distance of $0.6^\circ$.

Since the adiabatic contributions $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the temperature fluctuations are given directly by the density contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$, we can say that the shape of the CMB anisotropy spectrum in Fig. 6 in the regime $\alpha < \alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is a direct imprint of the distribution $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}(R)$ of the density contrast as a function of the size $R$ of the region of overdensity at the epoch of CMB formation. This regime includes, among other things, the so-called acoustic peaks, which we can observe in the right part of the spectrum. On the contrary, the contributions $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect ($\alpha \gg \alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$) prevail in the extreme left part of the spectrum in Fig. 6, where we observe an approximately constant distribution of $\delta T$ as a function of the angular size $\alpha$ (and hence also of the linear size $R$) of the region of overdensity.

h) What dependence $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}(R)$ of the density contrast on the radius $R$ of the region of overdensity follows from the data in Fig. 6 in the regime $R \gg R_{\mathrm{crit}}$? [2 points]

The mutual distance at which these objects orbit decreases as a result of the radiation of energy by gravitational waves, until the objects merge. Gravitational waves were first directly detected in 2015 by the LIGO observatory, later complemented by the European VIRGO detector for better triangulation of sources and signal analysis, and in 2020 also by the Japanese KAGRA observatory. One of the most important potentially measurable parameters of gravitational waves is their frequency just before the merger of the objects. Its calculation will occupy us in this problem.

According to GR, gravity can be described by the so-called Einstein field equations. The first exact and simplest solution of Einstein's equations was provided by Karl Schwarzschild only 20 days after the publication of Einstein's work on general relativity. The Schwarzschild metric, as the solution is called, describes the geometry of spacetime outside a single spherically symmetric, non-rotating, uncharged body, such as a black hole. As we will see below, an analysis of the motion of bodies in such a spacetime will lead us to the derivation of a relation for the maximum frequency of gravitational waves that we measure before the merger of the components of a binary system formed by black holes.

But let us first consider motion in classical mechanics. Specifically, in order to facilitate the description of the motion of bodies in a general central field, we introduce the so-called effective potential energy $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)$, which is defined by the relation
$$E = \frac{1}{2}mv_r^2 + V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r), \qquad (1)$$
where $E = \text{const.}$ is the total mechanical energy, $m$ is the mass of the so-called test body (a body that by its presence does not affect the field in which it moves), $v_r$ is the radial component of the velocity $\vec{v}$ of the test body with respect to the centre of the field and $r$ is the distance of the test body from the centre. Note that in relation (1) for the total mechanical energy only the kinetic energy of the radial motion appears explicitly; we have absorbed the kinetic energy of the angular motion into the effective potential energy $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)$ using the law of conservation of angular momentum.

where $\omega$ is the instantaneous angular velocity of the motion of the test body.

When light passes through a dust cloud, two phenomena therefore occur simultaneously: an overall attenuation of the starlight (extinction) and a change of its colour, the so-called interstellar reddening.

To measure the colour of objects precisely we use photometric observations in different filters. In this problem we will use the classical Johnson–Morgan system of broad-band filters U (ultraviolet), B (blue) and V (visual). The quantities $U$, $B$ and $V$ represent the observed magnitudes in the respective filters. The difference of the magnitudes in two filters gives a colour index, here specifically $B - V$ and $U - B$. In the colour–colour diagram the stars are therefore shifted by reddening along the so-called reddening line with slope
$$\frac{E(U-B)}{E(B-V)} \approx 0.72. \qquad (2)$$

where $\sigma_x = \sum_i x_i$, $\sigma_y = \sum_i y_i$, $\sigma_{xy} = \sum_i x_i y_i$, $\sigma_{xx} = \sum_i x_i^2$ and $\sigma_{yy} = \sum_i y_i^2$.

In the next part you will determine the velocity dispersion of one galaxy on the basis of measured optical spectra. The different radial velocities of the stars in a galaxy and their directions cause shifts of their spectral lines through the Doppler effect. When the spectra of all components are averaged, the spectral lines in the optical spectra of the galaxy are therefore broadened. This broadening and any shift are used to determine the dispersion by the cross-correlation method, which compares the similarity of the shape of the optical spectrum of the observed galaxy with a reference signal of a star of the spectral type corresponding to the majority of the population of the galaxy. These spectra are shifted relative to each other, and at each shift their mutual similarity is followed by means of their convolution. This is tracked by the so-called correlation function (see footnote 1).
